cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. A.W.
cases.holding: Reversing termination, the Court set out the four-part best-interests standard for terminating parental rights under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-15(c) and held the Division must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: The child's health and development have been or will be seriously impaired by the parental relationship.

relevance.OUT-02: A.W. is the source of New Jersey's four-prong best-interests test and its clear-and-convincing burden for terminating parental rights.
relevance.ACT-03: A.W. holds that removal and placement must be justified by proof of serious harm from the parental relationship, not by the family's poverty or social disadvantage.
relevance.ACT-04: A.W. states that when a relative is willing to provide long-term care, termination is 'unnecessary and unwise,' making relative placement a required alternative to consider.
relevance.OUT-03: A.W. treats long-term relative care as an alternative permanency arrangement that can make termination unnecessary.
relevance.OUT-06: A.W. arose after the death of an infant sibling in the home and shows how a fatality reframes the harm analysis for the surviving children.
relevance.FAIL-04: A.W. shows a court reviewing agency conduct after a child's death in a family already known to the Division.
relevance.PMC-04: A.W. illustrates judicial fatality review of agency records, criticizing illegible and inadequate Division case records.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of K.H.O.
cases.holding: The Court reinstated termination, holding a child born drug-addicted whose mother cannot care for her at birth is endangered under prong one and that the four statutory criteria overlap rather than operate discretely.
cases.quote: We hold that a child's health and development are endangered when she is born drug addicted and her mother cannot care for her at birth.

relevance.OUT-02: K.H.O. is the Supreme Court's controlling construction of each prong of N.J.S.A. 30:4C-15.1(a) in termination cases.
relevance.OUT-01: K.H.O. explains that a parent's continuing inability to overcome addiction and assume care defeats reunification and supports permanency.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of D.M.H.
cases.holding: The Court reversed the Appellate Division and reinstated termination, holding that the Division's reunification efforts are measured by their adequacy in the circumstances, not by whether they succeeded.
cases.quote: These efforts must be assessed against the standard of adequacy in light of all the circumstances of a given case.

relevance.OUT-01: D.M.H. sets the standard by which the Division's reunification efforts are judged before permanency is changed.
relevance.ACT-01: D.M.H. measures voluntarily offered services by their adequacy in the circumstances rather than by the parent's eventual success.
relevance.ACT-02: D.M.H. defines the 'diligent efforts' the Division must make under a court-ordered service plan.

cases.case_name: G.S. v. Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court held that the 'minimum degree of care' in N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.21(c)(4) means grossly or wantonly negligent conduct, not ordinary negligence, and affirmed the neglect finding against a caregiver who recklessly over-medicated a child.
cases.quote: the phrase "minimum degree of care" refers to conduct that is grossly or wantonly negligent, but not necessarily intentional

relevance.DEC-03: G.S. supplies the culpability standard every substantiated neglect finding in New Jersey must satisfy.
relevance.DEC-01: G.S. marks the line below which conduct is mere negligence and a report should not be substantiated.
relevance.OUT-06: G.S. arose from a serious medication injury to a child in a group-home setting and defines when such an injury is legally neglect.

cases.case_name: Department of Children & Families, Division of Youth & Family Services v. T.B.
cases.holding: The Court reversed a substantiated neglect finding and ordered the mother's name removed from the Child Abuse Registry because leaving a child briefly without confirming a grandparent was home was negligent but not grossly negligent.
cases.quote: every failure to perform a cautionary act is not abuse or neglect.

relevance.DEC-03: T.B. holds that a substantiation must rest on gross negligence or recklessness, not on an ordinary parenting lapse.
relevance.FAIL-01: T.B. is the leading example of a court vacating an agency substantiation and ordering registry removal.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Department of Children & Families v. A.L.
cases.holding: The Court reversed an abuse-or-neglect finding based on prenatal cocaine use, holding Title 9 requires competent proof of actual harm to the child or of imminent danger or substantial risk of harm.
cases.quote: If an expectant mother's drug use causes actual harm to the physical, mental, or emotional condition of a newborn child, a finding of abuse or neglect is appropriate.

relevance.DEC-05: A.L. defines the proofs the Division must be able to present before it files and litigates a Title 9 complaint.
relevance.DEC-04: A.L. requires evidence of actual harm or imminent danger, the same showing that must underlie an emergency removal.
relevance.INP-12: A.L. holds that suspicion of drug exposure alone does not establish the imminent danger needed to justify protective custody.
relevance.INP-05: A.L. discusses the Title 30 route for offering services to a family where no Title 9 finding can be made.
relevance.INP-07: A.L. addresses how hospital toxicology results at birth may and may not support a maltreatment finding.
relevance.DEC-06: A.L. points to voluntary Title 30 services as the correct response when the statutory harm threshold is not met.
relevance.OUT-05: A.L. resulted in dismissal of the finding because the record lacked proof of harm or risk.
relevance.FAIL-01: A.L. is the Supreme Court's reversal of an agency finding unsupported by competent evidence of harm.
relevance.FAIL-02: A.L. establishes the evidentiary threshold whose absence makes state intervention into the family unlawful.

cases.case_name: Department of Children & Families v. E.D.-O.
cases.holding: The Court held that imminent risk is measured at the time of the triggering event but that a categorical approach is improper, and remanded the mother's substantiation to the Office of Administrative Law for a hearing on the totality of the circumstances.
cases.quote: We also hold that the Division should have referred the mother's appeal to the OAL for a hearing.

relevance.DEC-03: E.D.-O. entitles a parent contesting a substantiated finding to an individualized OAL hearing rather than categorical treatment.
relevance.INP-10: E.D.-O. shows that escalation from report to substantiation must rest on a fact-specific evaluation of the whole situation.
relevance.DEC-06: E.D.-O. warns against automatic substantiation of single-incident conduct that may be handled without court action.
relevance.FAIL-01: E.D.-O. vacates the agency's summary disposition and remands for the hearing due process requires.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Child Protection & Permanency v. Y.N.
cases.holding: The Court reversed an abuse-or-neglect finding based solely on a newborn's methadone withdrawal, holding that a mother's participation in a prescribed, bona fide treatment program is not parental fault.
cases.quote: N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.21(c)(4)(b) does not require a finding of abuse or neglect when an addicted woman, who learns that she is pregnant, seeks timely professional treatment for her addiction

relevance.INP-07: Y.N. governs referrals generated by hospital reports of neonatal withdrawal symptoms.
relevance.INP-05: Y.N. protects a parent who seeks treatment on her own initiative from having that help treated as evidence of neglect.
relevance.ACT-06: Y.N. holds that following medically prescribed treatment, including methadone maintenance, cannot itself be the basis for a maltreatment finding.

cases.case_name: Division of Youth & Family Services v. G.M.
cases.holding: The Court held that after a Title 9 abuse-or-neglect finding the parent is entitled to a dispositional hearing on whether the children may safely be returned, and remanded because none was held.
cases.quote: upon a finding of abuse and neglect, the offending parent or guardian is entitled to a dispositional hearing

relevance.OUT-01: G.M. requires a hearing on safe return before the court continues a child's out-of-home placement.
relevance.ACT-02: G.M. frames the court's authority to order services and supervision at disposition following a finding.
relevance.ACT-03: G.M. holds that continued foster placement after a finding requires a dispositional hearing, not automatic continuation.
relevance.ACT-05: G.M. describes the preliminary protective orders available under N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.31 pending disposition.
relevance.INP-04: G.M. arose from a court-supervised Title 9 proceeding and defines the judicial steps that follow agency intervention.
relevance.DEC-05: G.M. maps the statutory sequence a petition sets in motion, from fact-finding to disposition.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Department of Children & Families v. I.S.
cases.holding: The Court held that a Title 9 action must be dismissed when no abuse or neglect is proved, but that jurisdiction may continue where the Division also proceeds under Title 30 to secure needed services for the child.
cases.quote: when the Division brings its complaint also under the authority granted to it under Title 30, the court's jurisdiction may continue

relevance.ACT-01: I.S. explains that N.J.S.A. 30:4C-11 services rest on parental consent, the statutory basis for a voluntary service plan.
relevance.ACT-02: I.S. identifies N.J.S.A. 30:4C-12 as the route for court-ordered services where no abuse or neglect finding exists.
relevance.DEC-06: I.S. authorizes a services-only path that avoids a Title 9 finding while still protecting the child.
relevance.DEC-05: I.S. tells the Division which statutory authority its petition must invoke for the relief it seeks.
relevance.INP-04: I.S. sets the limits on what a court may order the Division to do when a case is referred for assessment.
relevance.INP-05: I.S. addresses the voluntary-consent pathway a parent uses when asking the Division for help.
relevance.OUT-05: I.S. requires dismissal of the Title 9 case when the abuse-or-neglect allegation is not sustained.
relevance.OUT-01: I.S. permits continued Title 30 services to support a child after the Title 9 case ends.
relevance.ACT-05: I.S. delineates the conditions a court may impose on a parent under Title 30 short of removal.
relevance.OUT-04: I.S. is the Court's fullest statement of the Division's Title 30 authority to provide services to children in need, the authority underlying continued support of older youth.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. B.R.
cases.holding: The Court held that a parent in a termination case is entitled to effective assistance of counsel measured by the Strickland standard and raised on direct appeal, but affirmed because counsel's performance was not ineffective.
cases.quote: Either way, the performance of that counsel must be effective.

relevance.FAIL-01: B.R. creates the procedure for challenging a termination judgment on the ground that appointed counsel was ineffective.

cases.case_name: N.J. Division of Child Protection & Permanency v. R.L.M. (In re R.A.J.)
cases.holding: The Court held that under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-15.4 a parent may proceed pro se in a termination action, subject to timely and unequivocal invocation and the court's discretion to appoint standby counsel.
cases.quote: The parent's right of self-representation, however, is by no means absolute.

relevance.OUT-02: R.L.M. governs a parent's choice between appointed counsel and self-representation in a termination trial.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. P.P.
cases.holding: The Court held kinship legal guardianship is available only when adoption is neither feasible nor likely, so it cannot be raised as a defense to termination where a relative is willing to adopt.
cases.quote: when the permanency provided by adoption is available, kinship legal guardianship cannot be used as a defense to termination of parental rights under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-15.1a(3)

relevance.OUT-03: P.P. is the controlling New Jersey decision on when kinship legal guardianship, rather than adoption, is the permanency outcome.
relevance.ACT-04: P.P. explains the statutory role of kinship caregivers and when their care becomes a permanent legal arrangement.
relevance.OUT-04: P.P. describes kinship legal guardianship as lasting until the child turns eighteen or finishes secondary school, the state-law analogue to extended care.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. R.G.
cases.holding: The Court reinstated the trial court's denial of guardianship, holding that incarceration alone, without particularized evidence of its effect on each best-interests prong, cannot support termination.
cases.quote: we hold that the trial court's finding that the Division failed to prove its case by clear and convincing evidence is supported by the trial evidence

relevance.OUT-02: R.G. controls termination cases involving incarcerated parents and requires prong-by-prong proof rather than reliance on the fact of imprisonment.

cases.case_name: S.C. v. New Jersey Department of Children and Families
cases.holding: The Court upheld the Department's 'not established' investigative category but required improved notice, a credible-evidence basis, and an informal opportunity to respond, while rejecting any right to a contested OAL hearing.
cases.quote: We reject that due process considerations require the Department to conduct an adjudicative contested case proceeding either internally or at the Office of Administrative Law for a "not established" finding.

relevance.DEC-01: S.C. governs the consequences of closing an investigation short of substantiation, including non-expungement of the record.
relevance.DEC-02: S.C. describes the four possible investigative outcomes and the evidence needed for each.
relevance.DEC-03: S.C. contrasts the formal hearing rights that attach to substantiated findings with the informal process for 'not established' findings.
relevance.INP-08: S.C. arises from an investigation of alleged corporal punishment reported through school and child-protection channels.
relevance.INP-10: S.C. sets the notice a parent must receive when an intake becomes a formal investigative finding.
relevance.FAIL-06: S.C. details the statutory circumstances in which confidential 'not established' records may nonetheless be disclosed.
relevance.PMC-01: S.C. is judicial review of the Department's own regulatory outcome categories, the data on which state performance is measured.
relevance.PMC-03: S.C. shows external review of agency investigative standards prompted by parents, advocates and bar amici.
relevance.PMC-05: S.C. addresses public and inter-agency access to child-protection investigation records.
relevance.PMC-06: S.C. supplies the taxonomy of investigative findings that any cross-state data analysis of New Jersey outcomes must use.

cases.case_name: State v. Perricone
cases.holding: The Court upheld an order taking temporary custody of an infant and authorizing a blood transfusion over the parents' religious objection, finding no federal or state constitutional violation.
cases.quote: We hold, therefore, that neither N. J. S. A. 9:2-9 nor the action of the trial court pursuant to the statute is violative of either the Federal or the State Constitution.

relevance.ACT-06: Perricone is New Jersey's foundational authority for court-authorized emergency medical treatment of a child over parental objection.
relevance.INP-12: Perricone upholds temporary protective custody of a child where delay would endanger life.
relevance.DEC-04: Perricone shows the parens patriae basis on which the State may act immediately to protect a child's life.

cases.case_name: State v. P.Z.
cases.holding: The Court held that a father's statement to a DYFS caseworker during a Title 9 investigation was voluntary and not the product of custodial interrogation, so it was admissible in his criminal prosecution.
cases.quote: We conclude that defendant's statement to Kobran was not coerced in violation of his Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.

relevance.INP-03: P.Z. governs the coordination between child-protection caseworkers and prosecutors in a joint abuse investigation.
relevance.INP-01: P.Z. begins with a hospital's mandated report of a child's injuries and traces what follows from it.
relevance.INP-07: P.Z. shows the sequence set off when treating physicians report suspicious injuries to the Division.
relevance.DEC-02: P.Z. defines the limits on caseworker questioning of a parent once an investigation is accepted.

cases.case_name: State v. Michaels
cases.holding: The Court held that coercive or suggestive interview techniques can so taint a child's statements that a pretrial hearing on reliability is required before the child's statements or testimony may be admitted.
cases.quote: If a child's recollection of events has been molded by an interrogation, that influence undermines the reliability of the child's responses as an accurate recollection of actual events.

relevance.DEC-02: Michaels sets the standard for how children must be interviewed once an abuse investigation is accepted.
relevance.INP-03: Michaels governs joint law-enforcement and child-protection forensic interviewing of child witnesses.
relevance.INP-08: Michaels arose from disclosures in a day-care setting and shows how adult questioning can shape a child's report.

cases.case_name: J.D. v. M.D.F.
cases.holding: The Court reversed a final restraining order, holding that harassment requires proof of a purpose to harass and that the court must find the order necessary to protect the victim, with due-process protection for an unprepared defendant.
cases.quote: A history of domestic violence may serve to give content to otherwise ambiguous behavior and support entry of a restraining order.

relevance.ACT-05: J.D. states the findings a New Jersey court must make before issuing a protective order that restrains contact within a family.

cases.case_name: Brennan v. Bergen County Prosecutor's Office
cases.holding: The Court held OPRA required disclosure of the names and addresses of successful bidders at a government auction because the privacy clause did not shield that information, and reversed the denial of access.
cases.quote: OPRA favors broad public access to government records.

relevance.PMC-05: Brennan is the Supreme Court's current statement of the presumption of access to New Jersey government records under OPRA.
relevance.PMC-02: Brennan supports public access to the financial records that audits and oversight depend on.
relevance.PMC-06: Brennan supplies the access rule that makes state-level data collection and analysis possible.
relevance.FAIL-06: Brennan shows that an agency's refusal to release non-exempt records is itself reversible under OPRA.
relevance.INP-09: Brennan enables outside oversight by guaranteeing access to government records absent a specific exemption.

cases.case_name: F.A. v. W.J.F.
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court held that the immunity in N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.13 for persons who report suspected child abuse must be broadly and liberally construed in favor of the reporter, barring the suit against them.
cases.quote: We hold that immunity shall be broadly and liberally construed in favor of the reporting person.

relevance.INP-01: F.A. is the controlling New Jersey construction of the statutory immunity that protects mandated reporters from suit.
relevance.INP-02: F.A. applies N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.13 immunity to any person who reports, not only designated professionals.
relevance.INP-06: F.A. protects reporters whose hotline or informal reports turn out to be unfounded.

cases.case_name: In re Allegations of Physical Abuse at Blackacre Academy
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court upheld the Institutional Abuse Investigation Unit's substantiated finding, holding the unit could report its results to the Department of Education and the affected parents and was not required to hold a hearing first.
cases.quote: the IAIU was not required to conduct a formal or informal hearing before placing appellants' names in the Central Registry

relevance.INP-08: Blackacre governs investigations of abuse allegations against staff in school and institutional settings.
relevance.INP-09: Blackacre describes the institutional-abuse oversight unit and its duty to report findings to the licensing department.
relevance.DEC-03: Blackacre addresses the process due before a substantiated institutional finding is entered in the Central Registry.
relevance.FAIL-06: Blackacre confirms the agency's statutory authority to disseminate investigative findings to regulators and parents.
relevance.PMC-03: Blackacre illustrates independent institutional-abuse review operating outside the ordinary family court process.
relevance.PMC-05: Blackacre sets the limits on sharing confidential investigation reports with other agencies and affected families.

cases.case_name: N.J. Department of Children & Families v. R.R.
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court reversed a 'not established' finding as unsupported by the record and directed that the allegation be deemed 'unfounded' so the records would be treated accordingly.
cases.quote: As we find that the Division erred in finding the allegation was "not established," the Division shall deem the allegation to be "unfounded" and treat the records accordingly.

relevance.DEC-01: R.R. shows that even a closure short of substantiation must have record support or be converted to 'unfounded' and expunged.
relevance.DEC-03: R.R. applies arbitrary-and-capricious review to the Division's investigative findings.
relevance.INP-06: R.R. reviews the evidentiary sufficiency of an intake allegation that never rose above suspicion.
relevance.INP-10: R.R. polices the step from allegation to recorded finding.
relevance.OUT-05: R.R. is the remedy a parent obtains when the agency's finding cannot be sustained.
relevance.FAIL-01: R.R. is an appellate reversal of an agency finding, with a direction that the records be expunged.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. K.L.W.
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court reversed a termination judgment because the Division failed to comply with its statutory duty under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-12.1 to identify and assess relatives, which distorted the best-interests analysis.
cases.quote: The Division has a statutory obligation to contact relatives of a child in its custody.

relevance.ACT-04: K.L.W. is the leading New Jersey decision on the Division's duty to locate, notify and assess relatives as placement resources.
relevance.ACT-03: K.L.W. holds that non-relative foster placement cannot stand unexamined where identified relatives were never assessed.
relevance.OUT-03: K.L.W. requires the court to consider relative adoption or kinship legal guardianship before terminating parental rights.

cases.case_name: N.J. Division of Child Protection & Permanency v. M.C. (In re J.C.-R.)
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court affirmed in camera review and limited disclosure of a parent's confidential juvenile records for use in child-welfare litigation, subject to a protective order against wider dissemination.
cases.quote: That authority should be exercised subject to a protective order to prevent dissemination of those records outside of that confidential setting.

relevance.FAIL-06: M.C. sets the procedure that governs when confidential child-welfare and juvenile records may lawfully be released.
relevance.PMC-05: M.C. shows that confidentiality is overcome only by in camera review and a protective order, not by unrestricted disclosure.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of J.O.
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that ICWA's notice obligation was not triggered on this record and that no remedial program could have cured the father's sexual abuse of the children.
cases.quote: The notice obligation is triggered when the court "knows or has reason to know that an Indian Child is involved" in custody proceedings.

relevance.INP-11: J.O. is the published New Jersey decision on when ICWA notice and its heightened standards apply in a state child-welfare case.
relevance.FAIL-05: J.O. applies the federal anti-bias protections ICWA creates for Indian children and their tribes in state placement decisions.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. C.H.
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court held the trial judge's sua sponte dismissal of the abuse-or-neglect complaint mid-hearing violated due process and remanded, while affirming the dismissal that followed a noticed motion.
cases.quote: the court's sua sponte dismissal of the abuse or neglect complaint against C.H. was a due process violation necessitating a remand

relevance.OUT-05: C.H. sets the procedural conditions under which a dependency case may properly be dismissed.
relevance.FAIL-01: C.H. reverses a judicial disposition entered without notice and an opportunity to be heard.
relevance.DEC-05: C.H. protects the Division's right to present its full case once a petition is filed.
relevance.INP-04: C.H. describes the court's role and its limits once a child-protection matter is before it.

cases.case_name: L.A. v. New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court defined the standard governing a physician's statutory duty to report, holding 'reasonable cause to believe' exists when a probable inference from the available information is that the child's condition results from abuse.
cases.quote: The inference need not be the "most probable," but it must be more than speculation or suspicion.

relevance.INP-01: L.A. gives New Jersey's operative definition of the 'reasonable cause to believe' that triggers the duty to report.
relevance.INP-02: L.A. explains that the reporting threshold is deliberately low so that potential cases reach the Division for investigation.
relevance.INP-07: L.A. states the standard a treating physician must apply when deciding to report suspected abuse.
relevance.INP-12: L.A. discusses the statute allowing a physician or hospital to take immediate protective custody of a child.
relevance.ACT-06: L.A. addresses the medical setting in which emergency protective custody and treatment decisions are made.
relevance.DEC-04: L.A. supplies the inference standard that separates actionable suspicion from speculation before the State intervenes.
relevance.OUT-06: L.A. arose from civil claims after a child was seriously injured following an unreported or under-investigated presentation.
relevance.FAIL-04: L.A. examines whether professionals and the Division met their duties before a child came to further harm.
relevance.PMC-04: L.A. is a judicial post-mortem on missed reporting opportunities of the kind fatality reviews examine.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. A.G.
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of the rights of parents with serious mental illness, holding the Law Against Discrimination does not supply a defense in a termination case although the Division must still make reasonable efforts accommodating a parent's disability.
cases.quote: reliance upon the LAD is misplaced in the context of a termination of parental rights case

relevance.FAIL-05: A.G. is the New Jersey decision on disability-discrimination claims by parents in child-welfare proceedings and on the accommodation the Division must nonetheless provide.
relevance.ACT-01: A.G. evaluates whether the services offered were adequate for parents whose disabilities limit their ability to use them.
relevance.ACT-02: A.G. holds that court-ordered service plans must account for a parent's disability even though the LAD is no defense.

cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children and Youth Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment for the caseworker, holding that forcing a father from his home on the basis of an uncorroborated anonymous tip violated the family's constitutional right to integrity because there were no objectively reasonable grounds to suspect abuse.
cases.quote: Even considered together, minor inconsistencies which provide no affirmative evidence of sexual abuse cannot alone establish the objectively reasonable grounds necessary to remove a family member from the family unit.

relevance.FAIL-02: Croft is the Third Circuit's controlling authority that separating a family without objectively reasonable grounds is actionable under § 1983.
relevance.DEC-04: Croft sets the evidentiary floor a caseworker must have before effecting an emergency separation.
relevance.INP-12: Croft holds that an anonymous tip alone cannot justify taking a child or excluding a parent from the home.
relevance.INP-02: Croft addresses the weight that may be given to an uncorroborated third-party report.
relevance.INP-06: Croft is the leading circuit case on acting upon an anonymous hotline tip.
relevance.INP-03: Croft describes the coordination of a Childline report with police and agency investigators.
relevance.DEC-02: Croft confirms that investigating a family does not itself violate the right to family integrity, but acting on nothing does.
relevance.INP-10: Croft marks the point at which an investigation may escalate to coercive action.
relevance.ACT-03: Croft governs the constitutional limits on placing a child outside the home without adequate grounds.

cases.case_name: Mammaro v. New Jersey Division of Child Protection & Permanency
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of qualified immunity to New Jersey caseworkers, holding no clearly established law made the temporary removal of a child on these allegations a substantive due process violation.
cases.quote: Accordingly, no Supreme Court precedent clearly establishes that D.M.'s temporary removal from her mother's custody violated substantive due process.

relevance.FAIL-02: Mammaro is the Third Circuit's New Jersey-specific qualified-immunity decision limiting damages claims for temporary removals.
relevance.DEC-04: Mammaro shows the narrow margin between a contestable removal decision and one that defeats immunity.
relevance.INP-12: Mammaro addresses the short-term protective custody of a child pending Family Part review.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a State may terminate parental rights, invalidating New York's fair-preponderance standard.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: Santosky fixes the federal constitutional burden of proof that New Jersey's termination standard implements.
relevance.FAIL-03: Santosky is the constitutional floor against which a state's termination procedures are measured for compliance.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held there is no automatic federal right to appointed counsel in termination proceedings; the Mathews factors are weighed case by case against a presumption that appointed counsel is required only where physical liberty is at stake.
cases.quote: It is against this presumption that all the other elements in the due process decision must be measured.

relevance.OUT-02: Lassiter is the federal baseline on appointed counsel in termination cases, which New Jersey exceeds by statute and by B.R.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held the Due Process Clause imposed no constitutional duty on the county to protect a child from his father's violence, even though the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial or other special relationship.
cases.quote: the Due Process Clauses generally confer no affirmative right to governmental aid, even where such aid may be necessary to secure life, liberty, or property interests

relevance.FAIL-04: DeShaney is the controlling federal rule limiting constitutional liability when a child is harmed while known to the agency.
relevance.OUT-06: DeShaney governs the federal claims that follow a child's death or serious injury in an open agency case.
relevance.FAIL-03: DeShaney confirms that federal remedies for systemic protective failures lie in statute and oversight, not the Due Process Clause.
relevance.PMC-04: DeShaney explains why fatality accountability depends on review commissions and state law rather than federal constitutional suits.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' requirement creates no privately enforceable right, so beneficiaries could not sue the state agency under the Act or § 1983.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.FAIL-03: Suter is the reason federal child-welfare compliance is enforced through HHS funding and review rather than private suits.
relevance.PMC-01: Suter explains why CFSR monitoring and program improvement plans, not litigation, are the federal compliance mechanism.
relevance.PMC-02: Suter locates accountability for misuse of Title IV-E funds in federal audit and oversight rather than beneficiary suits.
relevance.PMC-03: Suter underscores why statutory oversight bodies such as citizen review panels carry the enforcement burden.
relevance.PMC-06: Suter defines the legal limits of enforcement that any accountability analysis of state performance must take into account.
relevance.INP-09: Suter frames the federal review and funding levers that drive systemic audits of state agencies.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law and that the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction over the adoption of children domiciled on the reservation.
cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

relevance.INP-11: Holyfield is the Supreme Court's controlling decision on when ICWA strips a state court of jurisdiction over an Indian child.
relevance.FAIL-05: Holyfield explains that ICWA was enacted to end discriminatory state removal practices against Indian families.

cases.case_name: In re the Guardianship of J.C.
cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination and remanded, holding that where termination rests on the child's bond with foster parents rather than current unfitness, the Division must prove by clear and convincing evidence, through a qualified expert who also evaluates the child's relationship with the natural parent, that separation would cause serious and enduring harm.
cases.quote: DYFS must prove by clear and convincing evidence that separating the child from his or her foster parents would cause serious and enduring emotional or psychological harm.

relevance.OUT-02: J.C. is the foundational New Jersey decision on the fourth best-interests prong, setting the bonding and psychological-parent proofs a termination judgment must rest on.
relevance.OUT-01: J.C. requires the court to weigh parallel evidence of the child's relationship with the natural parent, so that a bond formed during foster care cannot by itself defeat reunification.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. F.M.
cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination of a mother's parental rights, holding that substantial and credible evidence supported each of the four best-interests prongs, including that her inability to shield the children from their dangerous father satisfied prongs one and two and that the Division's enumerated services satisfied the reasonable-efforts prong.
cases.quote: Ultimately, a child has a right to live in a stable, nurturing environment and to have the psychological security that his most deeply formed attachments will not be shattered.

relevance.OUT-02: F.M. is the Court's most comprehensive modern restatement of the four-prong best-interests test and the deference owed to the family court's termination judgment.
relevance.OUT-01: F.M. states that a parent's failure to remove the danger posed by the other parent defeats reunification even where the Division's services were extensive.
relevance.ACT-02: F.M. measures the adequacy of a court-ordered service plan by the steps the Division actually took toward reunification, not by whether they succeeded.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. M.M.
cases.holding: The Court reversed the Appellate Division and reinstated the termination of the father's parental rights, holding that appellate review of a Family Part termination judgment is limited and that the trial court's findings, supported by adequate and credible evidence, were entitled to deference.
cases.quote: A reviewing court should uphold the factual findings undergirding the trial court's decision if they are supported by "adequate, substantial and credible evidence" on the record.

relevance.FAIL-01: M.M. is the controlling statement of when a Family Part child-welfare fact-finding may and may not be disturbed on appeal, the threshold every reversal argument must clear.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. P.W.R.
cases.holding: The Court reversed the abuse-or-neglect finding, holding the record inadequate to establish a Title 9 violation and that an occasional slap to a teenager's face as discipline, causing no bruising or marks, is not 'excessive corporal punishment' under N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.21(c)(4)(b).
cases.quote: Limiting state involvement only to interference with excessive corporal punishment requires the exercise of judgment by reviewing courts before a finding of physical abuse is entered against a parent.

relevance.DEC-03: P.W.R. supplies the substantive corporal-punishment standard that a substantiated physical-abuse finding in New Jersey must satisfy.
relevance.DEC-01: P.W.R. shows that conduct the Division itself labelled 'unfounded' cannot later be converted into a finding of physical abuse.
relevance.INP-08: P.W.R. arose from a report routed through school and family channels about slapping and is the substantive standard governing such school-sourced discipline referrals.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. G.L.
cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination and ordered reunification, holding DYFS failed to prove the statutory prongs where the mother had never harmed the child and complied with every requirement, and that the fourth prong is a fail-safe against termination rather than an independent basis for it.
cases.quote: That prong serves as a fail-safe against termination even where the remaining standards have been met.

relevance.ACT-03: G.L. holds that removing a child from a compliant, non-offending parent on the theory that she might someday give the other parent access was improvident and cannot support continued placement.
relevance.OUT-01: G.L. orders prompt reunification on an accelerating, professionally supervised visitation schedule after an unjustified removal.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. E.P.
cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of an unfit mother's parental rights to her emotionally fragile twelve-year-old daughter, holding the Division failed to prove on the fourth prong that severing the child's only enduring bond would not do more harm than good when adoption was a remote prospect.
cases.quote: We hold that the family court was clearly mistaken in finding that the Division satisfied the four-prong best-interests-of-the-child test and in terminating Andrea's relationship with her mother.

relevance.OUT-02: E.P. limits termination where permanency through adoption is unlikely, and is the Court's fullest treatment of an older, troubled child's own attachments and therapeutic needs in the best-interests analysis.
relevance.OUT-04: E.P. is the closest New Jersey Supreme Court authority to the aging-out problem, addressing a child likely to remain in foster care to majority and refusing to sever her last family tie to chase a remote adoption.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. A.R.G.
cases.holding: The Court affirmed as modified and remanded for de novo reconsideration, holding that 'aggravated circumstances' excusing the Division from reasonable reunification efforts under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-11.3 is a fact-specific inquiry and that a parent must first receive notice of the underlying facts and theory the State will rely on.
cases.quote: Moreover, any circumstances that increase the severity of the abuse or neglect, or add to its injurious consequences, equates to "aggravated circumstances."

relevance.ACT-02: A.R.G. defines the narrow circumstances in which a court may relieve the Division of its statutory duty to provide reunification services, and what notice the parent is owed first.
relevance.DEC-05: A.R.G. requires the State's pleading to outline the facts and theory supporting a waiver of reunification efforts before the court may make that finding.
relevance.INP-08: A.R.G. begins with an anonymous call to a school nurse who verified the child's bruises and reported to DYFS, illustrating the school-based intake pathway.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. V.T.
cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
cases.holding: The court reversed a neglect finding based on a father's positive cocaine and marijuana tests at two supervised visits, holding that drug use without expert proof of impairment or of actual or imminent harm to the child does not establish neglect.
cases.quote: Contrary to the trial judge's conclusion, use of illegal drugs days prior to a supervised visit does not as a matter of law constitute neglect.

relevance.INP-07: V.T. governs referrals generated by a parent's positive urine screens taken in the course of court-ordered treatment and supervised visitation.
relevance.DEC-03: V.T. is the Appellate Division companion to A.L. and Y.N., holding a substantiation cannot rest on drug use alone absent proof of risk to the particular child.
relevance.DEC-06: V.T. holds that relapse during treatment calls for continued services rather than a Title 9 finding, since imperfect recovery does not equate to abuse or neglect.

cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Child Protection and Permanency v. J.R.-R.
cases.holding: The Court reversed and remanded for a new hearing, holding that Title 9 nowhere authorizes shifting the burden of proof to parents to disprove culpability and that the family court's use of conditional res ipsa loquitur denied the parents a fundamentally fair hearing.
cases.quote: The family court's mistaken conception that the burden of proof shifted to Jenny and George rendered its factfindings fatally flawed and denied the parents a fundamentally fair hearing.

relevance.DEC-03: J.R.-R. is the most recent Supreme Court statement of the proofs required for a substantiated finding, barring the Division from substantiating against multiple caregivers by burden-shifting when it cannot prove who caused the harm.
relevance.DEC-02: J.R.-R. confirms that the Division carries the burden of persuasion throughout an investigation and fact-finding, and that a parent need not prove non-culpability.

cases.case_name: Doe v. Poritz
cases.holding: The Court upheld the constitutionality of Megan's Law registration and community notification but held that the registrant's interests in nondisclosure and in reputation are protectible liberty interests entitling him, on application, to judicial review before notification occurs.
cases.quote: We find that both interests constitute protectible liberty interests, and therefore that procedural protection is due.

relevance.DEC-03: Poritz supplies New Jersey's due-process framework for listing and disseminating a stigmatizing state finding about an individual, the analysis that underlies Central Registry challenges.
relevance.FAIL-06: Poritz holds that where the State discloses stigmatizing information it must build in procedural protection, so the disclosure regime itself is judicially reviewable.
relevance.PMC-05: Poritz is the leading New Jersey decision reconciling public disclosure of government-held information about individuals with the privacy and reputational interests that disclosure burdens.

cases.case_name: Stanley v. Illinois
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed the dependency adjudication, holding that an unwed father was entitled under the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses to a hearing on his fitness before the State could take his children from him.
cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

relevance.FAIL-02: Stanley is the foundational federal holding that removing a child from a parent without a fitness hearing violates due process, the premise on which § 1983 unlawful-removal claims rest.
relevance.DEC-04: Stanley requires an individualized determination of parental fitness rather than a presumption, and fixes the hearing the State owes when it takes custody.
relevance.INP-12: Stanley limits how long protective custody may continue without a hearing on the parent's fitness.
relevance.ACT-03: Stanley holds that a child may not be placed in state care on a categorical presumption about the parent, without proof and a hearing.

cases.case_name: Haaland v. Brackeen
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed Congress's constitutional authority to enact the Indian Child Welfare Act and reversed on the anticommandeering claims, vacating and remanding the equal-protection and nondelegation claims with instructions to dismiss for lack of standing.
cases.quote: But the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing.

relevance.INP-11: Brackeen is the controlling federal backdrop for any ICWA analysis today, confirming that ICWA validly binds state courts and agencies handling Indian child custody proceedings.
relevance.FAIL-05: Brackeen leaves the equal-protection challenge to ICWA's Indian-family placement preferences undecided for want of standing, so those anti-bias preferences remain enforceable.
relevance.ACT-04: Brackeen restates that ICWA requires a state court to place an Indian child with an Indian caretaker when one is available, controlling kinship and tribal placement decisions.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener and its opinion text read in this session; each quote is an exact substring of the majority (or per curiam) opinion, with whitespace and quotation marks normalized, and none comes from a syllabus, concurrence or dissent.

The key_cases currently in the NJ node files are keyword-matched noise (e.g. 'In re Opinion No. 735 of the Supreme Court Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics', 'In the Matter of the Estate of Jones', school-district and utility matters); none survived verification. The only genuine candidates in that list were DCPP v. D.C.A., DCPP v. J.C. and K.C., DCPP v. B.P. and S.C. v. DCF. Only S.C. v. DCF was retrieved, read and retained: the CourtListener clusters for the other three contain only the Clerk's syllabus, which the law-firm standard forbids quoting.

S.C. v. New Jersey Department of Children and Families has no reporter citation in its CourtListener cluster, so it is given in slip form using the Supreme Court docket (A-57-18, Court docket no. 081870). Counsel should confirm the official reported citation before filing.

OUT-04 (extended foster care / aging out) is the weakest node for New Jersey. No published New Jersey appellate decision construing N.J.S.A. 30:4C-2.3 or the Chafee/FCSIAA extension of care to age 21 was found in CourtListener. The two cases mapped -- I.S. (scope of the Division's Title 30 authority to serve children in need) and P.P. (kinship legal guardianship running to age eighteen or completion of secondary school) -- are the closest published authority. The one decision located squarely on aging out, Monmouth County Div. of Social Services ex rel. DYFS v. C.R., 316 N.J. Super. 600 (1998), was written by a judge of the Tax Court temporarily assigned at the trial level and was excluded as trial-court authority.

No published New Jersey decision was found applying the Fourth Amendment to a caseworker's warrantless entry of a home, to a caseworker's search of a child, or to interviewing a child at school without parental consent. Those points are carried by the controlling federal circuit for New Jersey (Croft and Mammaro, 3d Cir.). A New Jersey practitioner should expect to argue this ground on federal authority.

ICWA authority in New Jersey is thin. In re Guardianship of J.O. (App. Div. 2000) is the only published state decision retrieved, and it addresses the notice trigger, not active efforts, qualified expert witnesses, placement preferences or transfer to tribal court; INP-11 is therefore carried largely by the federal standard (Holyfield). J.O. predates the 2016 BIA ICWA regulations and Haaland v. Brackeen (2023), both of which must be checked before relying on it.

PMC-01 through PMC-06 are oversight/transparency nodes with no direct New Jersey case law. They are served by the governing federal enforceability rule (Suter v. Artist M.), New Jersey's OPRA and record-confidentiality decisions (Brennan, M.C., Blackacre) and S.C. v. DCF. No decision involving Citizen Review Panels, CFSR program improvement plans, or an HHS OIG / Single Audit finding against New Jersey was located. The same gap affects FAIL-03 (federal compliance failure), which rests on Suter, Santosky and DeShaney rather than on state authority.
No published New Jersey decision was found about children who go missing from foster care; no node's case list covers that subject.

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. All New Jersey cases cited are published (N.J. or N.J. Super. reporter citations given). Some CourtListener slip texts retain a 'NOT FOR PUBLICATION' banner from the original slip even where the opinion was later approved for publication; the reporter citations given here confirm publication.

On the Title 9 merits, four cases must be read together: G.S. (minimum degree of care means gross or wanton negligence) and T.B. (mere negligence is not neglect) supply the culpability element; A.L. (actual harm, imminent danger or substantial risk) and Y.N. (no fault where the mother follows prescribed treatment) supply the harm and fault elements. Any DEC-03, DEC-05 or FAIL-01 analysis in New Jersey turns on these four.
Lassiter's date_decided is given as the date stated in the opinion (June 1, 1981); the CourtListener cluster metadata carries 1981-08-28 for the same cluster, apparently an amended-opinion date.

The agency was the Division of Youth and Family Services (DYFS) until June 2012 and is now the Division of Child Protection and Permanency (DCPP) within the Department of Children and Families; pre-2012 case names in this brief refer to the same agency.

Blackacre Academy (1997) holds that no hearing is required before an institutional substantiation is entered in the Central Registry. It should now be read alongside E.D.-O. (2015), which requires an individualized OAL hearing for a contested substantiated finding, and S.C. (2020), which requires notice and an informal opportunity to respond for a 'not established' finding; where they conflict, the Supreme Court cases control.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Guardianship of J.C., 129 N.J. 1, 608 A.2d 1312 (1992) — verified via CourtListener citation lookup. The Supreme Court's foundational treatment of bonding, the psychological-parent relationship and the expert proofs required on the fourth best-interests prong. Its absence is the single largest gap in the OUT-02 cluster: a brief that cites A.W., K.H.O. and D.M.H. but not J.C. is missing the case the fourth prong actually runs on.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. F.M., 211 N.J. 420, 48 A.3d 1075 (2012) — verified. The Court's most comprehensive modern restatement of the four best-interests prongs and of the Division's reasonable-efforts obligation. Any current New Jersey termination brief leads with F.M.; the brief's newest TPR authority is R.G. (2014) and R.L.M. (2018), neither of which restates the standard. Belongs at OUT-02 and OUT-01.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. M.M., 189 N.J. 261, 914 A.2d 1265 (2007) — verified. The controlling statement of the standard of appellate review of Family Part fact-findings in child-welfare cases. Every node in the FAIL family that turns on whether a finding can be disturbed on appeal (FAIL-01 especially) needs it.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. P.W.R., 205 N.J. 17, 11 A.3d 844 (2011) — verified. Holds that an occasional slap on a teenager's face is not 'excessive corporal punishment' under N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.21(c)(4). This is the corporal-punishment case, and its absence is conspicuous at DEC-03 and INP-08, where S.C. (itself a corporal-punishment investigation) is mapped without the substantive standard that governs it.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. G.L., 191 N.J. 596, 926 A.2d 320 (2007) — verified. Title 9 neglect and the limits on the Division's response; already relied on inside K.L.W., which the brief cites, but never cited in its own right. Belongs at DEC-03 and ACT-03.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. E.P., 196 N.J. 88, 952 A.2d 436 (2008) — verified. Termination as to an older, troubled child, and the Court's treatment of the child's own wishes and therapeutic needs in the permanency analysis. Belongs at OUT-02 and is the closest the New Jersey Supreme Court comes to the concerns behind OUT-04.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. A.R.G., 179 N.J. 264, 844 A.2d 977 (2004) — verified. Supreme Court termination decision addressing the interplay of the prongs and the timing of permanency. Belongs at OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. V.T., 423 N.J. Super. 320, 32 A.3d 1145 (App. Div. 2011) — verified. Holds that a parent's drug use, without proof of resulting harm or imminent risk to the child, does not establish neglect. It is the Appellate Division companion to A.L. and Y.N. and should appear at INP-07, DEC-03 and DEC-06.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Child Protection & Permanency v. J.R.-R. (N.J. Dec. 2021) (Supreme Court docket 083807; CourtListener cluster carries no reporter citation — counsel must supply it) — verified to exist via CourtListener search. Holds the Division cannot substantiate against multiple caregivers by burden-shifting where it cannot prove which one caused the harm. This is the most recent Supreme Court word on the proofs required for a substantiated finding and is absent from DEC-03 and FAIL-01 entirely.

Missing (for a later pass): Doe v. Poritz, 142 N.J. 1, 662 A.2d 367 (1995) — verified. The New Jersey due-process framework for registry listing and disclosure of stigmatizing state findings; it is discussed inside Brennan, which the brief cites, and it underlies the registry due-process arguments at DEC-03 and PMC-05 that the brief currently leaves unsupported.

Missing (for a later pass): Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) — verified. The foundational federal holding that a parent's interest in the care and custody of his children is protected by the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses and cannot be extinguished without a hearing. It is cited inside Mammaro, which the brief relies on, yet appears nowhere in the brief. Belongs at FAIL-02, DEC-04 and OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — verified. Rejects the constitutional challenges to ICWA and is now the controlling federal backdrop for any ICWA analysis. The brief's own notes flag that J.O. must be checked against it, but it is not in the case list. INP-11 and FAIL-05 should not be filed without it.

Missing (for a later pass): Charlie H. v. Whitman, 83 F. Supp. 2d 476 (D.N.J. 2000) — verified case name and citation via CourtListener. The federal class action over New Jersey's child-welfare system that produced decades of consent-decree monitoring. It is a district court decision and so falls outside the brief's published-appellate rule, but it is the single most important systemic-oversight authority specific to New Jersey, and the PMC-01, PMC-02, PMC-03 and FAIL-03 nodes are effectively empty without at least acknowledging it.

GAP-CLOSING PASS (2026-09-21): all thirteen authorities flagged in the 'Missing (for a later pass)' notes above were searched for on CourtListener in this session, retrieved, read in full opinion text, and added below. Those thirteen notes are now closed and are retained only as an audit trail; where a detail in them proved inaccurate on retrieval, the correction is recorded in the notes that follow.

Added In re the Guardianship of J.C., 129 N.J. 1, 608 A.2d 1312 (1992) for OUT-02 and OUT-01: it is the Supreme Court's foundational treatment of bonding and psychological parenting, requiring clear and convincing expert proof of serious and enduring harm from separation and parallel proof of the child's relationship with the natural parent before the fourth prong can be satisfied. Quote taken from the lead opinion of Justice Handler (opinion 9693730), not from the Clifford concurrence.

Added N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. F.M., 211 N.J. 420, 48 A.3d 1075 (2012) for OUT-02, OUT-01 and ACT-02: it is the Court's most comprehensive modern restatement of the four best-interests prongs, of the reasonable-efforts inquiry, and of the deference owed to the family court, and is the case a current New Jersey termination brief leads with.

Added N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. M.M., 189 N.J. 261, 914 A.2d 1265 (2007) for FAIL-01: it supplies the 'adequate, substantial and credible evidence' standard that governs whether a Family Part child-welfare finding can be disturbed on appeal, the threshold every reversal argument in the FAIL family must clear. Quote taken from the Zazzali lead opinion (9759290), not the Wallace dissent.

Added N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. P.W.R., 205 N.J. 17, 11 A.3d 844 (2011) for DEC-03, DEC-01 and INP-08: it is the controlling corporal-punishment decision, holding that an occasional slap to a teenager's face leaving no marks is not 'excessive corporal punishment', and it now supplies the substantive standard that S.C. (a corporal-punishment investigation) was mapped at INP-08 and DEC-03 without.

Added N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. G.L., 191 N.J. 596, 926 A.2d 320 (2007) for ACT-03 and OUT-01: the Court held the removal of a compliant, non-offending mother's child was improvident, ordered reunification on an accelerating supervised-visitation schedule, and held the fourth prong is a fail-safe against termination rather than an independent basis for it. Note the correction below: G.L. is a termination (Title 30) case, not the Title 9 neglect case the earlier note described, so it is mapped at ACT-03 and OUT-01 rather than DEC-03.

Added N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. E.P., 196 N.J. 88, 952 A.2d 436 (2008) for OUT-02 and OUT-04: the Court reversed termination on the fourth prong where adoption was a remote prospect and the child's only enduring bond was with her mother, making it both a limit on termination and the closest New Jersey Supreme Court authority to the aging-out concerns behind OUT-04. Quote taken from the Albin lead opinion (9647564), not the Rivera-Soto dissent.

Added N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. A.R.G., 179 N.J. 264, 845 A.2d 106 (2004) for ACT-02, DEC-05 and INP-08: it defines 'aggravated circumstances' under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-11.3 excusing the Division from reunification efforts, and sets the notice a parent must receive before that finding. CORRECTION to the earlier note: A.R.G. is not a decision on the interplay of the best-interests prongs or the timing of permanency; on retrieval its holding is the aggravated-circumstances/reasonable-efforts-waiver standard plus a due-process notice template, so it is mapped accordingly and not at OUT-02. CORRECTION to the citation: the CourtListener cluster reports 179 N.J. 264, 845 A.2d 106 (2004), not 844 A.2d 977.

Added N.J. Division of Youth & Family Services v. V.T., 423 N.J. Super. 320, 32 A.3d 578 (App. Div. 2011) for INP-07, DEC-03 and DEC-06: it is the Appellate Division companion to A.L. and Y.N., holding that positive drug screens at supervised visits, absent expert proof of impairment or risk to the particular child, do not establish neglect. CORRECTION to the citation and date: the cluster reports 32 A.3d 578 (not 32 A.3d 1145) and a decision date of December 21, 2011.

Added N.J. Division of Child Protection and Permanency v. J.R.-R., No. A-56/57-19 (N.J. Sept. 27, 2021) for DEC-03 and DEC-02: a unanimous Court held that Title 9 nowhere authorizes shifting the burden of proof to parents to disprove culpability, rejecting the conditional res ipsa loquitur paradigm of In re D.T. It is the most recent Supreme Court word on the proofs required for a substantiated finding. CORRECTION to the earlier note: the decision date is September 27, 2021 (argued November 9, 2020), not December 2021; the cluster still carries no reporter citation, so slip form is used with the Appellate docket A-56/57-19 (Court docket no. 083807) and counsel must supply the reported citation.

Added Doe v. Poritz, 142 N.J. 1, 662 A.2d 367 (1995) for DEC-03, FAIL-06 and PMC-05: the Court held that a registrant's interests in nondisclosure and in reputation are protectible liberty interests requiring procedural protection before the State disseminates a stigmatizing finding, which is the framework underlying Central Registry due-process arguments. Quote taken from the Wilentz lead opinion (9636417), not the Stein dissent.

Added Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) for FAIL-02, DEC-04, INP-12 and ACT-03: it is the foundational federal holding that a parent is entitled to a hearing on fitness before the State removes his children, and is the premise on which the Third Circuit removal cases already in this brief (Croft, Mammaro) rest. Quote taken from the White majority (9424810), not the Burger dissent. It is mapped at DEC-04 and ACT-03 rather than OUT-02, which is already oversubscribed; Santosky and Lassiter carry the federal standard at OUT-02.

Added Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) for INP-11, FAIL-05 and ACT-04: it rejects the constitutional challenges to ICWA and is the controlling federal backdrop against which In re Guardianship of J.O. (2000) must now be read, as this brief's own ICWA note required.

Added Charlie H. v. Whitman, 83 F. Supp. 2d 476 (D.N.J. 2000) for PMC-01, PMC-02, PMC-03, FAIL-03, FAIL-04 and ACT-03: it is the systemic federal class action against New Jersey's child-welfare system, holding the AACWA, CAPTA, MEPA and ADA claims not privately enforceable under Section 1983 while allowing children in state custody to proceed on substantive due process claims to reasonable protection from harm and to care consistent with competent professional judgment. EXCEPTION FLAGGED: this is a United States District Court decision and therefore falls outside this brief's published-appellate-authority rule. It is included because the PMC-01, PMC-02, PMC-03 and FAIL-03 nodes have no New Jersey appellate authority at all, and because Charlie H. is the single most important systemic-oversight decision specific to this state. Counsel should cite it as persuasive district-court authority only, and should check the subsequent history (see Charlie v. Whitman, 213 F.R.D. 240 (D.N.J. 2003), the class-certification decision in the same litigation) before relying on it.

Every named authority the verifier flagged was located, retrieved and read; none had to be recorded as unverifiable. No candidate in the verifier's list turned out to be non-existent or off point, although the substance of A.R.G. and the parallel citations for A.R.G. and V.T. required the corrections noted above.

COVERAGE SWEEP (part 2): each of the six nodes that had fewer than two mapped cases before this pass was re-examined. INP-04 now also carries C.H. (428 N.J. Super. 40), whose relevance entry already claimed that node but which the node_map omitted. OUT-04 now carries I.S. and P.P. (both of whose relevance entries already claimed it) plus the newly added E.P. PMC-01 now carries S.C. and Charlie H. alongside Suter; PMC-02 carries Brennan and Charlie H.; PMC-03 carries S.C., Blackacre and Charlie H.; PMC-04 carries A.W. and L.A. alongside DeShaney. The same reconciliation restored B.R. (192 N.J. 301) to FAIL-01 and Brennan to INP-09, where they had likewise been orphaned.

Fresh searches were run in this session for the two weakest nodes to confirm the existing gap findings rather than rely on them. For OUT-04, CourtListener searches of the New Jersey Supreme Court and Appellate Division for extended foster care, continued Division custody to age 21, and N.J.S.A. 30:4C-2.3 returned no on-point published decision; OUT-04 therefore rests on I.S., P.P. and E.P., none of which construes the age-21 extension directly. For PMC-04, searches for New Jersey child fatality and near-fatality review board decisions returned nothing on point; PMC-04 therefore continues to rest on the federal standard (DeShaney) plus the two New Jersey decisions that perform judicial post-mortems on agency and professional conduct after a child's death or serious injury (A.W. and L.A.).

DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM THE 2-6 CASES-PER-NODE TARGET: two hub nodes now exceed six. OUT-02 carries nine (A.W., K.H.O., R.L.M., R.G., Santosky, Lassiter, J.C., F.M., E.P.) and DEC-03 carries ten (G.S., T.B., E.D.-O., S.C., Blackacre, R.R., P.W.R., V.T., J.R.-R., Doe v. Poritz). Trimming either to six would have required deleting already-verified mappings and would have orphaned cases that serve no other node (R.L.M., R.G. and Lassiter are mapped only at OUT-02). Because the instruction for this pass was to extend the node_map rather than prune it, and because these two nodes are the ones the verifier specifically identified as under-served, the existing mappings were preserved and the additions made on top. Every other node is within the 2-6 range.

Quote provenance for this pass: for each multi-opinion cluster the opinions endpoint was queried and the opinion type inspected, and quotes were drawn only from the opinion typed '020lead' or '010combined' authored by the Court. Dissents and concurrences retrieved in the same call (Clifford in J.C., Wallace in M.M., Rivera-Soto in E.P., LaVecchia in A.R.G., Stein in Doe v. Poritz, Burger in Stanley, Wallace in G.L.) were read to identify them and then excluded as quote sources. Every quote in the thirteen new entries was programmatically re-verified as an exact substring of its source opinion after normalizing whitespace, curly quotation marks and dashes.

One quote candidate was discarded for text-integrity reasons and is recorded here so the choice is auditable. The most quotable sentence in P.W.R. -- that a slap of the face of a teenager as a form of discipline, with no resulting bruising or marks, does not constitute excessive corporal punishment -- is interrupted in the CourtListener text by an OCR artifact, and the equivalent sentence in V.T. (that Title 9 is not intended to extend to all parents who imbibe illegal substances at any time) is interrupted by an embedded star-page marker. Rather than silently repair either, a different clean sentence carrying the same rule was quoted in each case, and the holding field states the rule the discarded sentence expresses.

Charlie H. v. Whitman is the only non-appellate decision in this brief. It is also the only entry from a federal district court. Both facts are deliberate and are flagged again here because a reader scanning the case list for authority weight must not mistake it for binding precedent: it binds no New Jersey court and no later federal court, and it is offered for the PMC and FAIL-03 nodes precisely because nothing of higher authority addresses them for this state.

Missing (for a later pass): In re D.T., 229 N.J. Super. 509 (App. Div. 1988) — the conditional res ipsa loquitur decision that J.R.-R. expressly repudiates. J.R.-R. is in the brief but D.T. is not, so the brief states the new rule without the rule it displaced; any adversary litigating a multi-caregiver substantiation will cite D.T., and counsel needs it in hand at DEC-02 and DEC-03.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Guardianship of J.N.H., 172 N.J. 440 (2002) — cited by name and page inside M.M., which the brief now relies on. It is a Supreme Court termination decision bearing on the limited scope of review and on expert proofs; FAIL-01 and OUT-02 both lean on M.M.'s deference formulation without the decision M.M. drew it from.

Missing (for a later pass): Cesare v. Cesare, 154 N.J. 394 (1998) — the general source of the deference owed to Family Part fact-finding and credibility determinations, cited inside M.M. FAIL-01 turns entirely on that threshold and currently carries only the child-welfare-specific statement of it.

Missing (for a later pass): Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997) — the governing framework for when a federal spending statute creates a right enforceable under Section 1983. Charlie H. applies it explicitly and the brief's own note says so, yet Blessing itself is absent. FAIL-03, PMC-01 and PMC-02 all rest on the enforceability question Blessing decides.

Missing (for a later pass): Youngberg v. Romeo, 457 U.S. 307 (1982) — the professional-judgment standard for persons in state custody. It is the source of the 'care consistent with competent professional judgment' duty that Charlie H. allowed to proceed, which is the entire content of FAIL-04's custodial-child theory.

Missing (for a later pass): Nicini v. Morra, 212 F.3d 798 (3d Cir. 2000) (en banc) — the controlling Third Circuit decision on a foster child's substantive due process right to protection from harm and the standard of culpability applied to caseworkers. It is the binding circuit law for New Jersey on the theory Charlie H. only allowed past a motion to dismiss; FAIL-04 should not be filed without it.

Missing (for a later pass): Miller v. City of Philadelphia, 174 F.3d 368 (3d Cir. 1999) — establishes the 'shocks the conscience' standard for substantive due process claims arising from child-welfare interventions in this circuit. Croft and Mammaro are both read through it, so FAIL-02 and DEC-04 are incomplete without the standard that governs them.

Missing (for a later pass): B.S. v. Somerset County, 704 F.3d 250 (3d Cir. 2013) — a New Jersey-adjacent circuit decision on removal without pre-deprivation process and the qualified immunity available to caseworkers. It post-dates Croft and pre-dates Mammaro and is the case an adversary will use to frame both; FAIL-02 and DEC-04 need it.

Missing (for a later pass): Good v. Dauphin County Social Services, 891 F.2d 1087 (3d Cir. 1989) — the Third Circuit's decision on a caseworker's warrantless entry and search in a child-abuse investigation. The brief's own notes identify the absence of Fourth Amendment authority as a known gap and say the point must be carried on federal law; this is the federal case that carries it, and nothing currently sits at that gap.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the Supreme Court's modern statement of the fundamental parental liberty interest in the care, custody and control of children. Santosky and Stanley are in the brief but the current articulation of the underlying right is not, and it is the framing authority for DEC-04, FAIL-02 and OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Guardianship of Cope, 106 N.J. Super. 336 (App. Div. 1969) — the long-standing New Jersey rule that a parent's poverty, lifestyle or social disadvantage is not itself a ground for severing the parental relationship. ACT-03's relevance sentence for A.W. asserts exactly this proposition, and Cope is the decision New Jersey courts cite for it.

Missing (for a later pass): N.J. Division of Child Protection & Permanency v. D.C.A., 256 N.J. 4 (2023) — the recent Supreme Court decision on excessive corporal punishment and substantiation. The brief's own notes identify D.C.A. as a genuine candidate that was excluded only because its CourtListener cluster carried a syllabus rather than the opinion text. It is the most current word at DEC-03 and INP-08 and should be retrieved from the reporter rather than dropped; counsel should confirm the reported citation before filing.
